chapter.name: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
chapter.blurb: The Iron Pillar, the rise and rulers of the Guptas, Faxian, governance and trade, science and literature, art, decline and neighbouring kingdoms.

scope_in.item: The Iron Pillar and the rise of the Guptas

concepts.name: The Iron Pillar of Delhi and the rise of the Guptas
concepts.description: The rust-free Iron Pillar, Chandragupta I and II, and how the Guptas emerged after the Kushanas.
concepts.idea: The Guptas rose as the Kushana empire weakened, and the Iron Pillar shows their metallurgical skill.
concepts.rule: The Iron Pillar of Delhi at Mehrauli is over 1,600 years old, weighs about 6 tonnes and does not rust because a thin protective layer forms on its surface. It was erected in the reign of Chandragupta II, probably first in front of the Udayagiri caves, and is dedicated to Vishnu. By the 3rd century CE the Kushana empire weakened and the Guptas, probably from near present-day Uttar Pradesh, rose. Chandragupta I laid the foundation through alliances; Chandragupta II, also called Vikramaditya, was a devotee of Vishnu whose mount is Garuda.
concepts.example: Historians add II to Chandragupta II because his grandfather was also Chandragupta.

concepts.name: Samudragupta, the warrior king
concepts.description: The Prayaga Prashasti, Samudragupta's conquests, coins and the extent of the Gupta empire.
concepts.idea: Samudragupta expanded the empire through war and diplomacy and is celebrated in the Prayaga Prashasti.
concepts.rule: The Prayaga Prashasti, a pillar inscription at Prayagraj written by the court poet Harisena, praises Samudragupta, Chandragupta II's father, whose ambition was to be dharani-bandha, to unify the Earth. He defeated many kings, took over some kingdoms, reinstated others who paid tribute, and supported art, learning and trade. A coin shows him playing the veena. The ashvamedha coin shows a sacrificial horse. The Vishnu Purana names key regions, but at its peak the empire covered most of north and west India and parts of central and east India.
concepts.example: One Samudragupta coin shows him playing the veena.

concepts.name: Faxian's account and how historians use sources
concepts.description: Faxian's visit, what he recorded, his blind spots and the need to compare sources.
concepts.idea: Traveller accounts are valuable but partial, so historians compare several sources.
concepts.rule: Faxian, a Chinese traveller, visited India in the early 5th century CE on a Buddhist pilgrimage to visit sacred sites, learn from scholars and collect manuscripts. He recorded a happy, numerous people who did not need to register households, farmers of royal land paying part of their grain, salaried royal guards, rich cities and charity houses for the poor and sick. He also described harsh treatment of the chandalas, regarded as outcastes. Accounts show only the writer's perspective, so historians study multiple sources, perspectives and interpretations.
concepts.example: Faxian's travelogue is called A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms.

concepts.name: Gupta governance, titles and trade
concepts.description: Royal titles, alliances such as Prabhavati Gupta, provincial administration, land grants and trade.
concepts.idea: The Guptas ruled through provinces, land grants and alliances and thrived on trade.
concepts.rule: Gupta rulers used titles such as maharajadhiraja, samrat and chakravartin to claim supreme authority, unlike earlier simpler titles like rajan and maharaja. They expanded through conquest, diplomacy and alliances, including marriages. Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, married a Vakataka prince and after his early death ruled as regent, keeping ties strong; she is linked to seven Vishnu temples. The empire was divided into provinces, land was granted to local rulers, priests and chieftains and recorded on copper plates. Land tax was the main revenue. The Guptas traded with the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China, and Socotra was a stop.
concepts.example: Land grants were inscribed on copper plates for accurate records.

concepts.name: The classical age: science, literature and medicine
concepts.description: Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Kalidasa, Ayurveda and why the period is called classical.
concepts.idea: Peace and patronage made the Gupta age a classical age of science, literature and medicine.
concepts.rule: Long peace and stability under the Guptas supported scholars, artists and scientists. Aryabhata of Kusumapura wrote the Aryabhatiya around 500 CE, proposed that the Earth spins on its axis, gave the year as 365 days 6 hours 12 minutes 30 seconds, and explained eclipses. Varahamihira of Ujjayini wrote the encyclopedic Brihat Samhita on astronomy, weather, architecture, town planning and farming. Kalidasa wrote Sanskrit poetry such as the Meghaduta, or Cloud Messenger. Ayurveda was codified: the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas took final shape.
concepts.example: Kalidasa's Meghaduta has a yaksha send a message to his beloved through a cloud.

concepts.name: Gupta art and the decline of the empire
concepts.description: Centres of Gupta art, Ajanta and Udayagiri, and how invasions and regional powers ended the empire.
concepts.idea: Gupta art set high standards of beauty, but Huna attacks and rising regional powers ended the empire.
concepts.rule: Gupta art flourished at Sarnath, known for Buddha sculptures, at the Ajanta caves in Maharashtra, supported by the Guptas and Vakatakas, and at Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh, with rock-cut caves and carvings of deities. Terracotta figures show Ganga standing on a makara and Yamuna on a tortoise. By the 6th century CE the Gupta empire declined as the fierce Huna tribe from Central Asia repeatedly attacked and powerful regional rulers caused internal conflicts.
concepts.example: A terracotta Ganga stands on a makara and Yamuna on a tortoise.

concepts.name: The Pallavas, Kamarupa and Gupta relations with neighbours
concepts.description: The Pallavas of Kanchipuram, the Varman kingdom of Kamarupa, and Samudragupta's tributary policy.
concepts.idea: The Pallavas in the south and the Kamarupa kingdom in the northeast flourished as cultural centres alongside the Guptas.
concepts.rule: The Pallavas rose after the Satavahanas and ruled from Kanchipuram, the city of a thousand temples, till the 9th century. Most were devotees of Shiva, built temples and rock-cut caves and supported ghatikas, centres of learning. The Kamarupa kingdom, ruled by the Varman dynasty, covered the Brahmaputra valley in present Assam and parts of Bengal and Bangladesh, with temples and monasteries as learning centres. Samudragupta defeated Pallava and Kamarupa rulers but let them keep their thrones if they accepted his rule and paid tribute.
concepts.example: Kanchipuram is known as the city of a thousand temples.
